summary: Describes Rabbit, a stream cipher with a 128-bit key and 64-bit initialization vector. Published in 2003 and publicly reviewed, it is fast and suits protocols that process large amounts of data. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Rabbit is a super-fast scrambler that turns messages into gibberish and back, using a secret key, so it works well on large amounts of data.

questions: fast stream cipher for internet protocols
subtitle: A fast encryption algorithm designed for protocols processing large amounts of data.

tldr.problem: Internet protocols that handle large volumes of data need encryption that is both very fast and mathematically secure, which is hard to achieve in traditional block ciphers.
tldr.mechanism: Rabbit is a stream cipher with a 128-bit key and 64-bit IV that generates a pseudorandom bit stream using iterative functions based on discretized chaotic maps. Encryption XORs plaintext with this stream and uses the same stream for decryption.
tldr.outcome: Rabbit offers high-speed encryption suitable for applications like server-side encryption, multimedia streaming, disk encryption, and constrained devices. It underwent public security review after publication in 2003.

today: RFC 4503 is Informational. Rabbit remains a fast, secure stream cipher that has not displayed weaknesses years after its publication. It is used in applications requiring high-speed encryption of large data volumes, though it has not become as widely adopted as some standardized encryption modes for block ciphers.

sections.title: Introduction to Rabbit
sections.content:
Rabbit is a stream cipher algorithm designed for high-speed software encryption. Unlike traditional block ciphers (which encrypt fixed-size chunks like 128 bits at a time and are slower), Rabbit generates a continuous stream of pseudorandom bits that can be mixed with plaintext byte by byte or bit by bit. This makes encryption and decryption very fast while using minimal memory.

Rabbit was published in 2003 and publicly reviewed through the ECRYPT eSTREAM project, a major cryptographic evaluation effort. It has not displayed any weaknesses as of this document's publication. The algorithm is particularly suited for applications that process large amounts of data: server-side encryption of files and databases, multimedia encryption, full-disk encryption, and encryption on devices with limited computational resources.
sections.eli5: Rabbit is fast because it generates scrambling keys on the fly as you encrypt, rather than stopping to do complicated math for each block. It is safe because many cryptographers have looked at it and found no flaws.

sections.title: How Rabbit Works
sections.content:
Rabbit uses a 128-bit (16-byte) secret key and a 64-bit (8-byte) initialization vector (IV). The IV allows the same key to be reused safely for multiple messages by changing the starting state each time. The algorithm maintains an internal state of 513 bits: eight 32-bit state variables (X0 through X7), eight 32-bit counter variables (C0 through C7), and one carry bit.

During key setup, the algorithm initializes the state and counter variables from the key, then iterates through a core function four times to thoroughly mix them. If an IV is provided, the counter variables are modified with the IV bits, and the algorithm iterates four more times to derive the encryption starting state.

For encryption, Rabbit repeatedly executes a counter update (adding special constants to the counter variables with overflow), a next-state function (applying the core transformation), and an extraction function that produces 128 bits of output. The encryption is simply: plaintext XOR the pseudorandom output. Decryption is identical: ciphertext XOR the same pseudorandom output. The security depends on the pseudorandom stream being unpredictable; attackers cannot forge encryption without knowing the key.
sections.eli5: The algorithm starts with your key and IV, then generates random-looking numbers in a special way that depends on the key. These numbers are mixed with your message to scramble it. The same mix on the scrambled message unscrambles it.

sections.title: The Core Transformation and State Update
sections.content:
The heart of Rabbit is a function g that takes two 32-bit inputs and produces one 32-bit output. It works by adding the inputs, squaring the result, then XORing the least significant and most significant 32 bits of that square. This g function is applied to each pair of state and counter variables to produce intermediate values.

These intermediate values are then combined (with rotations and additions) to update the eight state variables. The specifics of the rotation amounts and which variables combine with which are carefully chosen to provide strong mixing and avoid patterns that cryptanalysts could exploit.

The counter system increments special constants (patterns like 0x4D34D34D) through the counter variables with a carry bit, similar to how odometers roll over when they overflow. This ensures the counters advance in a predictable but non-trivial way.

The extraction scheme takes portions of the state variables and XORs them to create 128 bits of output per iteration. Which bits are selected and XORed together is designed so that an attacker cannot invert the process to recover the internal state from just the output.
sections.eli5: The algorithm does a series of mathematical operations on special numbers. It mixes them, carries over like an odometer, and extracts bits in a way that looks random but depends on the key. An attacker cannot reverse the process.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Proper Use
sections.content:
Rabbit can encrypt up to 2 to the power of 64 (approximately 18 quintillion) 128-bit message blocks under a single key. Once this limit is approached, the key must be replaced to prevent security weakening. This is an extremely large amount of data and is not a practical concern for most applications.

The initialization vector (IV) is critical for security when the same key is reused. An IV must never be repeated under the same key; doing so would destroy the cipher's security because the same pseudorandom stream would be used twice, allowing attackers to XOR the two ciphertexts and recover information about the plaintext. Applications using Rabbit must ensure that each (key, IV) pair is unique. Many practical systems reset the cipher with a new IV for each message and keep track of which IVs have been used.

When an IV is not used (the cipher runs continuously under the same key without reset), the generator must never be reset under that key. If it were reset, the stream would repeat, and the same security break would occur. Therefore, applications must choose: either use an IV and change it each time, or never reset without an IV. The RFC provides detailed test vectors to verify that implementations work correctly.
sections.eli5: The same key can scramble an enormous amount of data. But if you do not change the IV each time you use the same key, an attacker can compare two scrambled messages and learn things. So always change the IV or never reset the scrambler.
